title: Adversus Marcionem
author: Tertullian
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0275.stoa006.opp-lat2, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: ut ergo aliquid + et de isto huius mundi indigno loquar, cui et apud Graecos ornamenti et cultus, non sordium, nomen est, indignas uidelicet substantias ipsi illi sapientiae professores, de quorum ingeniis omnis haeresis animatur. deos pronuntiauerunt, ut Thales aquam, ut Heraclitus ignem, ut Anaximenes aerem. ut Anaximander uniuersa caelestia, ut Strato caelum et terram, ut Zeno aerem et aetherem, ut Plato sidera, quae genus deorum igneum appellat, cum de mundo, considerando scilicet et magnitudinem et uim et potestatem et honorem et decorem, opem fidem legem singulorum elementorum, quae omnibus gignendis alendis conficiendis reficiendisque conspirant, ut plerique physicorum, formidauerint, [initium ac finem mundo constare] ne substantiae eius, tantae scilicet, minus dei haberentur, quas colunt et Persarum magi et Aegyptiorum hierophantae et Indorum gymnosophistae.
passages.english: So, to say something also about this 'unworthy' [thing] of this world, which even among the Greeks has a name meaning ornament and adornment, not filth: those very professors of wisdom, from whose minds every heresy draws its life, declared these supposedly unworthy substances to be gods, as Thales [declared] water, as Heraclitus fire, as Anaximenes air, as Anaximander all the heavenly bodies, as Strato heaven and earth, as Zeno air and ether, as Plato the stars, which he calls the fiery race of gods; since concerning the world, considering, that is, the greatness and force and power and honour and beauty, the aid, reliability and law of the individual elements, which work together in begetting, nourishing, completing and renewing all things, most of the natural philosophers shrank from [maintaining that the world has a beginning and an end], lest its substances, being so great, should be held less divine; [substances] which the magi of the Persians and the hierophants of the Egyptians and the gymnosophists of the Indians worship.
passages.notes: The edition marks a crux (+) after 'aliquid'. The bracketed phrase 'initium ac finem mundo constare' is bracketed in the edition, perhaps as suspect or supplied; translated as part of the sense. Punctuation of the edition (full stop before 'deos') is awkward; the sentence has been read continuously.

passages.original: erit enim et locus deus, non tantum qua deo maior, sed et qua innatus et infectus ac per hoc aeternus et deo par, in quo semper deus fuerit. dehinc si et ille mundum ex aliqua materia subiacente molitus est innata et infecta et contemporali deo, quemadmodum de creatore Marcion sentit, redigis et hoc ad maiestatem loci, qui et deum et materiam, duos deos, clusit. et materia enim deus secundum formam diuinitatis, innata scilicet et infecta et aeterna, aut si de nihilo molitus est mundum, hoc et de creatore sentire cogetur, cui materiam subicit in substantiam mundi.
passages.english: For place will also be a god, not only in that it is greater than god, but also in that it is unborn and unmade and therefore eternal and equal to god, [place] in which god has always been. Next, if he too built the world out of some underlying matter, unborn and unmade and coeval with god, as Marcion holds concerning the creator, you reduce this too to the majesty of place, which has enclosed both god and matter, two gods. For matter too is a god according to the form of divinity, being, that is, unborn and unmade and eternal. Or if he built the world out of nothing, [Marcion] will be compelled to hold this also concerning the creator, to whom he assigns matter as the substance of the world.

passages.original: Huic expeditissimae probationi defensio quoque a nobis necessaria est aduersus obstrepitacula diuersae partis. aiunt enim Marcionem non tam innouasse regulam separatione legis et euangelii quam retro adulteratam recurasse. o Christe, patientissime domine, qui tot annis interuersionem praedicationis tuae sustinuisti, donec tibi scilicet Marcion subuenirct!
passages.english: To this most ready proof a defence is also necessary on our part against the clamourings of the opposing side. For they say that Marcion did not so much innovate the rule [of faith] by his separation of the law and the gospel as restore it after it had earlier been adulterated. O Christ, most patient Lord, who for so many years endured the perversion of your preaching, until, of course, Marcion came to your rescue!

passages.original: quem enim iudicem tenes, dispensatorem, si forte, bonitatis ostendis intellegendum, non profusorem, quod tuo deo uindicas. usque adeo hac sola eum praefers bonitate creatori. quam si solam profitetur et totam, nulli deesse debuerat. sed nolo iam de parte maiore pereuntium imperfectae bonitatis arguere deum Marcionis: sufficit ipsos, quos saluos facit, imperfectae salutis inuentos imperfectam bonitatem eius ostendere, scilicet anima tenus saluos, carne deperditos, quae apud illum non resurgit. unde haec dimidiatio salutis nisi ex defectione bonitatis?
passages.english: For the one whom you hold to be a judge, you show must be understood as, perhaps, a dispenser of goodness, not a squanderer of it, which is what you claim for your god. To such an extent do you prefer him to the creator on account of this goodness alone. If he professes this alone and in its entirety, he ought to have failed no one. But I will not now accuse Marcion's god of imperfect goodness on the grounds of the greater number of those who perish: it is enough that those very ones whom he saves, being found to have an imperfect salvation, show his goodness to be imperfect, saved, that is, as far as the soul, lost in the flesh, which with him does not rise again. Where does this halving of salvation come from, if not from a failure of goodness?

passages.original: si enim intercessisset, rescidisset arbitrii libertatem, quam ratione et bonitate permiserat. denique puta intercessisse, puta rescidisse illum arbitrii libertatem, dum reuocat ab arbore, dum ipsum circumscriptorem colubrum a congressu feminae arcet: nonne exclamaret Marcion: o dominum futtilem, instabilem, infidelem, rescindentem quae instituit? cur permiserat liberum arbitrium, si intercedit? cur intercedit, si permisit? eligat, ubi semetipsum erroris notet. (in) institutione an in rescissione.
passages.english: For if he had intervened, he would have annulled the freedom of choice which he had permitted out of reason and goodness. Suppose, then, that he had intervened, suppose he had annulled freedom of choice, by calling [man] back from the tree, by keeping the deceiving serpent himself from meeting the woman: would not Marcion cry out, 'O fickle, unstable, unfaithful lord, annulling what he instituted! Why had he permitted free choice, if he intervenes? Why does he intervene, if he permitted it?' Let him choose where he will brand himself with error: in the institution or in the annulment.

passages.original: Nunc et de pusillitatibus et malignitatibus ceterisque notis et ipse aduersus Marcionem antithesis aemulas faciam. si ignorauit deus meus esse alium super se, etiam tuus omnino non sciit esse alium infra se. quid enim ait Heraclitus ille tenebrosus? eadem uia sursum et deorsum. denique si + non ignorasset, et ab initio ei occurrisset. delictum et mortem et ipsum auctorem delicti diabolum et omne malum, quod deus meus passus est esse, hoc et tuus, qui illum pati passus est.
passages.english: Now, concerning the petty failings and the malicious acts and the other marks [charged against the Creator], I too will make rival antitheses against Marcion. If my God did not know that there was another [god] above him, your [god] also did not know at all that there was another below him. For what does that obscure Heraclitus say? "The way up and down is the same." Finally, if he had not been ignorant [of him], he would also have met him from the beginning. Sin and death and the author of sin himself, the devil, and every evil, which my God allowed to exist, this your [god] also [allowed], who allowed him to allow it.
passages.notes: The edition marks a crux (+) before "non ignorasset"; the sentence "denique si non ignorasset, et ab initio ei occurrisset" is probably corrupt and its sense is uncertain. The final sentence is elliptical; "[allowed]" is supplied. "sciit" is an irregular perfect for "sciuit".

passages.original: hoc enim Marcion ut additum erasit. sed frustra negabit Christum dixisse quod statim fecit ex parte. prophetiam enim interim de loco adimpleuit: de caelo statim. ad synagogam. ut dici solet: \'ad quod uenimus, hoc age\\ Marcion: aufer etiam illud de euangelio: non sum missus nisi ad oues perditas domus Israhel, et: non est auferre panem filiis et dare eum canibus, ne scilicet Christus Israhelis uideatur. sufficiunt mihi facta pro dictis.
passages.english: For Marcion erased this as an addition. But in vain will he deny that Christ said what he at once partly did. For he fulfilled the prophecy meanwhile as to place: from heaven, at once to the synagogue. As the saying goes: 'Get on with what we came for.' Marcion, remove also this from the gospel: 'I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,' and: 'It is not [right] to take the children's bread and give it to the dogs,' so that, of course, Christ may not seem to be Israel's. Deeds suffice me in place of words.

passages.original: Praestruximus quidem aduersus antithesis nihil proficere proposito Marcionis quam putat diuersitatem legis et euangelii. ut et hanc a creatore dispositam, denique praedicatam in repromissione nouae legis et noui sermonis et noui testamenti. sed quoniam adtentius argumentatur apud illum suum nescio quem ouvTaXawutopov (commiseronem) et auvp.iao6(x=vov (coodibilem) in leprosi purgatione, non pigebat ei occurrere et inprimis figuratae legis uim ostendere, quae in exemplo leprosi non contingendi, immo ab omni commercio summouendi, communicationem prohibebat hominis delictis commaculati, cum qualibus et apostolus cibum quoque uetat sumere;
passages.english: We have indeed already laid down, against the Antitheses, that what Marcion considers the difference between law and gospel does nothing for his purpose, since this too was arranged by the Creator, and indeed foretold in the promise of a new law, a new word and a new covenant. But since he argues more pointedly before that fellow-sufferer (commiseronem) and co-hated one (coodibilem) of his, whoever he is, in the cleansing of the leper, it was no trouble to meet him, and first of all to show the force of the figurative law, which, in the example of the leper who was not to be touched, indeed was to be removed from all dealings, forbade association with a person stained by sins, with whom the apostle forbids even taking food;
passages.notes: The Greek words are garbled in the scan; they correspond to the Latin glosses given, roughly synталaipōros 'fellow-sufferer' and symmisoumenos 'co-hated'. The 'ut et hanc' clause is elliptical.

passages.original: quapropter septies, quasi per singulos titulos, in Iordane lauit, simul ut et totius hebdomadis caneret expiationem et quia unius lauacri uis et plenitudo Christo soli dicabatur, facturo in terris sicut sermonem compendiatum ita et lauacrum. nam et hoc opponit Marcion: Heliseum quidem materia eguisse, aquam adhibuisse, et eam septies, Christum uero uerbo solo, et hoc semel functo, curationem statim repraesentasse. quasi non audeam et uerbum ipsum in substantiam creatoris uindicare: nullius rei non ille potior auctor, qui prior.
passages.english: For this reason he washed seven times in the Jordan, as if once for each charge, both so as to proclaim the expiation of the whole seven, and because the force and fullness of a single washing was reserved for Christ alone, who was to bring about on earth an abridged washing, just as [he would bring] an abridged word. For Marcion objects this too: that Elisha needed a material, applied water, and that seven times, whereas Christ, by a word alone, and using it once, effected the cure immediately. As if I would not dare to claim the word itself also for the substance of the creator: he is the more authoritative author of everything who is first.
passages.notes: 'titulos' taken as the seven capital sins listed in the preceding context.

passages.original: quodsi et auctoritas diuina et rerum natura et communis sapientia non admittunt insaniam haereticam, occasio est et hic interpellandi quam breuissime de substantia corporis aduersus phantasmata Marcionis. si natus ex homine est, ut filius hominis, corpus ex corpore est. plane facilius inuenias hominem natum cor non habere uel cerebrum, sicut ipsum Marcionem, quam corpus, ut Christum Marcionis. atque adeo inspice cor Pontici aut cerebrum.
passages.english: But if divine authority, the nature of things and common wisdom do not admit this heretical madness, here too there is occasion to interject, as briefly as possible, about the substance of [Christ's] body, against Marcion's phantasms. If he was born of a human being, as son of man, he is body from body. Truly, you would more easily find a man born without a heart or brain, like Marcion himself, than [without] a body, like Marcion's Christ. And so, examine the heart or brain of the man from Pontus.

passages.original: nam sicut sanis medicum nemo adhibet, ita nec in tantum extraneis, quantum est homo a deo Marcionis, suum habens et auctorem et protectorem et ab illo potius medicum Christum. hoc similitudo praeiudicat, ab eo magis praestari medicum, ad quem pertinent qui languent. Unde autem et Iohannes uenit in medium? subito Christus, subito Iohannes. sic sunt omnia apud Marcionem, quae suum et plenum habent ordinem apud creatorem. sed de Iohanne cetera alibi. ad praesentes enim quosque articulos respondendum est. nunc illud tuebor, ut demonstrem et Iohannem Christo et Christum Iohanni conuenire, utique qua prophetae creatoris Christum creatoris, atque ita erubescat haereticus, Iohannes ordinem frustra frustratus. si enim nihil omnino administrasset Iohannes, secundum Esaiam uociferator in solitudinem et praeparator uiarum dominicarum per denuntiationem et laudationem paenitentiae, si non etiam ipsum inter ceteros tinxisset, nemo discipulos Christi manducantes et bibentes ad formam discipulorum Iohannis adsidue ieiunantium et orantium prouocasset, quia, si qua diuersitas staret inter Christum et Iohannem et gregem utriusque, nulla esset comparationis exactio, uacaret prouocationis intentio.
passages.english: For just as no one calls a physician for the healthy, so neither for those so utterly foreign as man is to Marcion's god, man who has his own author and protector, and from him rather [has] Christ as physician. The comparison prejudges this: that the physician is more likely provided by the one to whom the sick belong. But where does John too come on the scene from? Suddenly Christ, suddenly John. So it is with everything in Marcion, which with the creator has its own complete order. But the rest about John elsewhere; for we must answer each point as it arises. Now I will maintain this, to show that John agrees with Christ and Christ with John, precisely in that the creator's prophet [suits] the creator's Christ, and so let the heretic blush, having frustrated John's order in vain. For if John had administered nothing at all, as the one crying out in the wilderness according to Isaiah and the preparer of the Lord's ways by proclaiming and commending repentance, if he had not also baptized [Christ] himself among the rest, no one would have challenged Christ's disciples, eating and drinking, by the model of John's disciples, constantly fasting and praying; because, if there were any difference standing between Christ and John and the flock of each, there would be no demand for comparison, the thrust of the challenge would be void.
passages.notes: 'prophetae creatoris' read as 'propheta creatoris' (singular) for sense. 'Iohannes ordinem frustra frustratus' is difficult; perhaps read 'Iohannis'.

passages.original: neutra congruens domino (tuo.) denique: diuidetur, inquit, pater in filium et filius in patrem, et mater in filiam et filia in matrem, et nurus in socrum et socrus in nurum. hoc proelium inter parentes si in ipsis uerbis tuba cecinit prophetae, uereor ne Micheas Christo Marcionis praedicarit. Et ideo hypocritas pronuntiabat caeli quidem et terrae faciem probantes, tempus. uero illud non dinoscentes, quo scilicet, adimplens omnia, quae super ipso fuerant praedicata, nec aliter docens debuerat agnosci.
passages.english: Neither fitting for your lord. Then: 'Father,' he says, 'will be divided against son and son against father, and mother against daughter and daughter against mother, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law and mother-in-law against daughter-in-law.' If the prophet's trumpet sounded this battle among kinsfolk in these very words, I fear Micah preached for Marcion's Christ. And so he declared them hypocrites, who could judge the face of heaven and earth but did not discern that time in which, of course, fulfilling everything that had been foretold about him, and teaching nothing otherwise, he ought to have been recognized.
passages.notes: The opening fragment continues the previous discussion (sword and fire); its referent is unclear without it.

passages.original: aut si propterea panem corpus sibi finxit, quia corporis carebat uanitatem, ergo panem debuit tradere pro nobis. faciebat ad uanitatem Marcionis, ut panis crucifigeretur. cur autem panem corpus suum appellat et non magis peponem, quem Marcion cordis loco habuit, non intellegens ueterem fuisse istam figuram corporis Christi dicentis per Hieremiam: aduersus me cogitauerunt cogitatum dicentes: uenite. coiciamus lignum in panem eius, scilicet crucem in corpus eius? itaque inluminator antiquitatum, quid tunc uoluerit significasse panem, satis declarauit corpus suum uocans panemsic et in calicis mentione testamentum constituens sanguine suo obsignatum substantiam corporis confirmauit.
passages.english: Or if he feigned the bread to be his body because he lacked the reality of a body, then he ought to have handed over bread for us. It would have suited Marcion's empty fancy that bread should be crucified. But why does he call bread his body, and not rather a melon, which Marcion had in place of a heart? [Marcion did] not understand that this was an ancient figure of the body of Christ, who said through Jeremiah: "They devised a device against me, saying: Come, let us cast wood into his bread", that is, the cross into his body. And so he who sheds light on the things of old made plain enough what he had then meant the bread to signify, when he called his body bread. So too, in mentioning the cup and establishing the testament sealed with his blood, he confirmed the substance of his body.
passages.notes: "melon" (peponem): a jibe that Marcion had a melon for a heart, i.e. was witless. The last sentence is run together in the edition ("panemsic" = "panem. sic").

passages.original: legum enim et secundum nostrum euangelium diabolus quoque in temptatione cognouit, et secundum commune instrumentum spiritus nequam sciebat eum sanctum dei esse et Iesum uocari et in perditionem eorum uenisse. etiam parabola fortis illius armati, quem alius ualidior oppressit et uasa eius occupauit, ***, si in creatoris accipitur apud Marcionem, iam nec ignorasse ultra potuit creator dominum gloriae, dum ab eo opprimitur, nec in cruce eum figere, aduersus quem ualere non potuit, et superest, ut — secundum me quidem credibile sit — scientes uirtutes et potestates creatoris dominum gloriae, Christum suum, crucifixerint, qua desperatione et malitiae redundantia serui quoque scelestissimi dominos suos interficere non dubitant;
passages.english: For according to our gospel the devil too recognised him in the temptation, and according to the common scripture the evil spirit knew that he was the Holy One of God, that he was called Jesus, and that he had come for their destruction. Also the parable of that strong man armed, whom another stronger overpowered and seized his goods, ***; if in Marcion's version it is taken as referring to the Creator, then the Creator could no longer have been ignorant of the Lord of glory while he was being overpowered by him, nor [could he have] fixed on the cross one against whom he had no strength. And it remains that, as is credible at least in my view, the virtues and powers of the Creator crucified the Lord of glory, his Christ, knowingly, out of that despair and overflowing malice by which even the most wicked slaves do not hesitate to kill their masters;
passages.notes: The opening "legum" is likely corrupt (perhaps for "denique" or similar); rendered as "For". The edition marks a lacuna (***) after the parable clause; the sentence is incomplete there.

passages.original: hunc ascensum si Christus nobis praeparabit, ille erit Christus, de quo Osee: qui ascensum suum aedificat in caelos, utique sibi et suis. exinde a quo sperabo nunc, nisi a quo haec audiui ? Quem spiritum prohibet extingui et quas prophetias uetat nihil haberi? utique non creatoris spiritum nec creatoris prophetias secundum Marcionem. quae enim destruit, ipse iam extinxit et nihil fecit, nec potest prohibere quae ipse fecit. ergo incumbit Marcioni exhibere hodie apud ecclesiam suam exinde spiritum dei sui, qui non sit extinguendus, et prophetias, quae non sint nihil habendae.
passages.english: If Christ will prepare this ascent for us, he will be the Christ of whom Hosea [speaks]: "who builds his ascent into the heavens", surely for himself and his own. From whom then shall I now hope [for it], except from him from whom I heard these things? What Spirit does he forbid to be quenched, and what prophecies does he forbid to be held as nothing? Certainly not the Creator's Spirit nor the Creator's prophecies, according to Marcion. For what he destroys he has himself already quenched and made nothing, and he cannot forbid [to be done] what he himself has done. Therefore it falls to Marcion to produce today in his church, from that source, the Spirit of his god, which is not to be quenched, and prophecies which are not to be held as nothing.
passages.notes: The quotation attributed to Hosea is actually from Amos 9:6.

passages.original: Quis autem est homo delicti, filius perditionis, quem reuelari prius oportet ante domini aduentum, extollens se super omne quod deus dicitur et omnem religionem, consessurus in templo dei et deum se iactaturus? secundum nos quidem antichristus, ut docent ueteres ac nouae prophetiae, ut Iohannes apostolus, qui iam antichristos dicit processisse in mundum, praecursores antichristi spiritus, negantes Christum in carne uenisse et soluentes Iesum, scilicet in deo creatore; secundum uero Marcionem nescio, ne Christus sit creatoris. nondum (enim) uenit apud illum. quisquis est autem ex duobus, quaero, cur ueniat in omni uirtute et signis et ostentis mendacii. propterea, inquit, quod dilectionem ueritatis non susceperint, ut salui essent;
passages.english: But who is the man of sin, the son of perdition, who must be revealed before the Lord's coming, exalting himself above all that is called god and above all religion, who is to sit in the temple of God and boast himself to be god? According to us, indeed, the Antichrist, as both the old and the new prophecies teach, and as the apostle John [teaches], who says that antichrists have already gone out into the world, forerunner spirits of the Antichrist, denying that Christ has come in the flesh and dissolving Jesus, that is, in God the Creator. But according to Marcion I do not know, unless it be the Creator's Christ; for in his view [that Christ] has not yet come. But whichever of the two he is, I ask why he comes with all power and signs and lying wonders. "Because," he says, "they did not receive the love of the truth, so that they might be saved";
passages.notes: "ne Christus sit creatoris" is obscure; rendered as "unless it be"; possibly corrupt ("nisi"?).
